newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobutu seeks four-day delay in talks with Kabila.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu seeks four-day delay in talks with Kabila.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Thursday Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko wanted four days' grace to study South African proposals for an orderly handover of power to the rebels waiting at the gates of his capital.

"We made certain proposals to him which he requested to take to Kinshasa to consult his advisers," Mandela told a news conference after 2-1/2 hours of talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila in Cape Town. "We are expecting an answer from him on Monday."
Asked at the news conference if he would refrain from marching into Kinshasa for a bloody showdown with Mobutu's troops, Kabila replied: "I have nothing to say about it."

Mandela said he had briefed Kabila on the talks he had with Mobutu in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire on Wednesday. Kabila had been due to attend the Congo meeting as well but pulled out at the last minute, citing security concerns.
"We are all waiting for the response from President Mobutu," Mandela said, refusing to give any details of his discussions with Kabila in Cape Town.
"Matters are going according to plan. We are confident a solution can be found because we have had cooperation from both parties....

"It is in the interests of the whole continent (that we find a settlement). Zaire has borders with nine different countries and instability has a ripple effect on all. For that reason it is absolutely crucial to bring about peace....
"We are confident we are making progress," Mandela said.
Kabila said he had little to add. "We shall wait till Monday to receive another answer from Mr Mobutu's side."
Earlier on Thursday, Kabila's rebels warned Mobutu to quit the capital before Saturday or risk capture by advancing forces.

Lisbon's Lusa news agency quoted rebel justice spokesman Mwenze Kongolo as saying: "The only way out of the crisis is for Mobutu to hand over power to the armed rebellion which will form a transitional government together with other forces fighting for the same cause."
Mobutu, his army in tatters, has few bargaining chips left and diplomats said his choices now amounted to picking the best face-saving way to hand over power.

Fighting cancer and the encircling grip of Kabila's rebel alliance, the ageing dictator returned to Kinshasa from Pointe Noire on Thursday. Witnesses said he spurned a red carpet farewell and honour guard laid on by the Congolese.
Zaire's teeming capital of five million grew more tense by the hour as residents braced for what many believe is the inevitable battle for Kinshasa and an orgy of looting by retreating soldiers.
Shops were shuttered and the normally bustling streets emptied ominously well before sundown and a third night of military curfew. The airport was effectively closed.
"We're heading directly for a bloodbath. It's a question of balance of forces. Kabila knows he has the upper hand," said Mobutu aide Kabuya Lumuna.
In a message broadcast by BBC World Service radio, the British Foreign Office urged British and Commonwealth nationals to leave the capital while commercial transport was available.
"The situation is increasingly volatile in the Kinshasa area," the broadcast said.
On the roof of the French embassy in downtown Kinshasa diplomatic staff were seen burning what appeared to be shredded documents.
A member of the Organisation of African Unity delegation in Pointe Noire told reporters on Thursday the OAU was very pessimistic about prospects for a negotiated peace.

South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, a key negotiator in the Zairean peace initiative, had said on Monday that Wednesday's scheduled three-way meeting in Pointe Noire could be Zaire's last chance for peace.

Despite Kabila's failure to attend, Mbeki and Mandela renewed their initiative, urging African and Western leaders to help rescue the talks and sending a jet to bring Kabila from the Angolan enclave of Cabinda to Cape Town.
Kabila and Mandela spoke for about an hour alone before being joined by U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun and Mbeki.
The South African Broadcasting Corporation, quoting a leaked copy of Mandela's proposal, said it would require Mobutu to step down within 24 hours of signing a settlement.
The European Parliament on Thursday urged Mobutu and Kabila to form an interim government to organise democratic elections.
